title: What Our Backtest Says About the Senate Model
dek: Our calibration page shows a model that is still being tested, not a model that is failing. The archived-input backtest is the better measure, while the other diagnostic is mostly a temporary stress test.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: A forecast model should do more than pick winners. It should also show whether its probabilities make sense.
If a model gives a candidate a 65 percent chance to win, candidates in that range should win around 65 percent of the time across many races. That is called calibration.
Our Senate model is still early in its calibration work. The page currently shows two different tests. That has created some confusion.

The most important test is the archived-input historical backtest. That is the cleaner test because it uses older, saved model inputs from past elections. It asks a simple question: if this model existed at the time, how close would it have been?
The archived-input test is the one readers should focus on most. It is closer to a real test of the model.

Right now, the archived-input sample is still small. It uses 11 races from the 2024 Senate cycle. That is not enough for a final verdict, but it is enough to see whether the model is behaving in a reasonable way.

So far, the archived-input results look solid. The 50 to 60 percent bucket went 2 for 2. The 60 to 70 percent bucket went 3 for 4. The 70 to 80 percent bucket went 2 for 2. The 80 to 90 percent bucket went 3 for 3.
That does not prove the model is perfect. Small samples can look cleaner than they are. But it does show the model is not behaving randomly. It is sorting races into reasonable probability ranges.
The second test on the page is the current diagnostic. That one has a larger 35-race sample, but it is not the same as the archived-input backtest.
The current diagnostic compares the live model shape against older Senate results. That makes it useful for finding weak spots, but it is not the main calibration grade.

This matters because some comparisons are imperfect. Some states are being compared to 2016 or 2018 races. Some states had very different candidates. Some had little polling. Some had unusual election rules or independent candidates.
That is why the current diagnostic should be read as a stress test. It helps us see where the model might need adjustment. It should not be treated as the final proof of whether the model works.

Even then, the current diagnostic does not show a broken model. The 60 to 70 percent bucket had a 62.5 percent historical win rate, compared with a 65 percent expected win rate. The 90 to 100 percent bucket had a 95 percent historical win rate, exactly matching its 95 percent expected win rate.

The weakest-looking area is the 80 to 90 percent bucket. In the current diagnostic, that bucket had a 33.3 percent historical win rate. But that bucket only had three races, so it should not be overread.

The archived-input margin misses also look normal for a Senate model. The largest misses were Pennsylvania at 5.2 points, Wisconsin at 4.2 points, Ohio at 3.6 points, Nebraska at 3.4 points, Nevada at 3.3 points, Florida at 2.8 points, Arizona at 2.6 points, and Montana at 2.1 points.

Those misses are not alarming. Senate races are hard to model. Candidate quality, incumbency, state polling, independent candidates, and late movement all matter. A few misses in the two to five point range are normal.

The current diagnostic also shows a mean Brier score of 0.143 and a mean margin miss of 12.5 points. The margin miss number looks high, but it comes from the less clean diagnostic, not the archived-input backtest.
That is the main source of confusion. One section is a cleaner historical backtest. The other section is a broader live diagnostic. Both are useful, but they do different jobs.
By May 23, 2026, we plan to finish the calibration cleanup and make the page easier to understand. The goal is to clearly separate the archived-input backtest from the current diagnostic.
After that update, readers should have a clearer answer to three questions. What is the true backtest? What is only a diagnostic? What should be used to judge the model?

The honest defense of the model is simple. It is not fully validated yet. More archived cycles are needed. Some probability buckets still have small samples. The current diagnostic has noisy comparisons.

But the evidence does not show a failed model. The archived-input backtest looks promising. The largest archived misses are within a normal range. Several probability buckets line up well with expected outcomes.

The model is still being improved, but the early signs are positive. The best way to read the page is simple: use the archived-input backtest as the main score, and use the current diagnostic as a warning system.
Once the May 23 calibration update is finished, the model will have a clearer and more direct way to show how accurate it is.

title: How Dan Osborn has Redefined the Democratic Strategy of the Deep Red
dek: Dan Osborn's Senate campaigns show a different path for Democrats in deep-red states. In places where the party label struggles, an independent with local credibility may perform better than a standard Democratic nominee.
author: Capitol Forecast

content.text: Dan Osborn has changed how you should think about deep-red Senate races.

Nebraska is not considered in any pathway to victory for Democrats in 2026 when it comes to the Senate. This is in large part because Republicans dominate the state. Democrats struggle in deep-red Nebraska due to negative brand recognition. AP reported that Nebraska Democrats in 2026 are looking for others who can "outperform the Democratic label."

Osborn is in a different form. He ran as an independent in 2024 and is running again in 2026. He leans on his background as a mechanic, Navy veteran, National Guardsman, and union leader. He campaigns on workers' rights, wages, corporate power, and taking money out of politics.

We saw what happened in 2024. Osborn lost to Republican Senator Deb Fischer, but the race was shockingly close historically in Nebraska. Fischer won by only about six points, while in 2024, the state voted for Donald Trump by over 20 points. What we learned was simple. Some voters who might reject national Democrats would still consider a candidate who sounds local, independent, and focused on economics.

Just last week, Cindy Burbank won the Democratic Senate primary in Nebraska. She campaigned simply on withdrawing and supporting Osborn. This reduces a split anti-Ricketts vote and avoids a three-way race, which all but guarantees Republicans hold on in the state.

Nebraska Democrats appeared to understand that when Nebraska's race focuses on the national aspect, Ricketts wins. When it goes local, Osborn stands to benefit. This is what Democrats need to study. Sometimes in a deep-red state, stepping aside is more strategic.

Of course, this does not work anywhere. You need someone with local credibility and a message voters believe. In a state where voters have histories of ticket splitting or independents, it might be the right move. However, national Democrats must stay disciplined. If these independents are turned into Republican versus not Republican, the brand is weakened.

Even if what the forecast model says holds, and Osborn loses, the current projected margin of only 3.9 points Republican shares a big message. Democrats must reinvent their strategies in the deep red, or become a figment of the past for those living in red states.
The takeaway should be clear. In deep-red states, Democrats need more flexibility. Sometimes the best Democratic move is to support a candidate who does not run as a Democrat.
